report:
**Conclusion:** Your impression is correct—current clinical evidence shows that taking coenzyme Q10 (CoQ10) does **not** improve movement disorders or slow functional decline in Parkinson's disease.

### Evidence Summary

* **The QE3 Phase III Trial:** A major randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study funded by the National Institutes of Health (NIH) evaluated high-dose CoQ10 (1,200 mg/day and 2,400 mg/day) in early Parkinson's disease. The trial was terminated early for futility because CoQ10 showed no evidence of clinical benefit or slowing of motor symptoms compared to placebo (https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamaneurology/fullarticle/1851409).
* **Systematic Reviews & Meta-Analyses:** Meta-analyses pooling data from multiple randomized controlled trials found no significant improvement in motor scores (measured via the Unified Parkinson's Disease Rating Scale) or daily function among patients taking CoQ10 versus placebo (https://europepmc.org/article/med/26553164; https://www.mdpi.com/2075-4426/12/6/975).
* **Official Health Guidance:** The National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health (NCCIH) notes that while CoQ10 is generally well tolerated, major clinical studies demonstrate that higher-than-usual doses do not improve Parkinson's symptoms (https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/coenzyme-q10).

Although CoQ10 was initially considered a promising neuroprotective candidate due to its role in cellular mitochondrial energy production, rigorous clinical testing has conclusively demonstrated that it does not alleviate Parkinson's movement disorders.
